items.title: fix(bot-desktop): a takeover counts as use of an idle screen
items.content:
fix(bot-desktop): a takeover counts as use of an idle screen

The idle stop times out a human lease nobody has used for four windows, judged by the screen's activity
stamp. A takeover did not stamp it; only the viewer's first RFB frame did. A takeover landing on a long-idle
screen while an idle check waited on start.lock was therefore read as an already abandoned lease: the
screen was stopped under the human who had just taken it, and their lease handed back to the agent.
display.lease.acquire now stamps activity before it writes the lease, as the idle section's comment already
said a takeover does: the new lease is visible to the screen's own idle check (and to this process's
listeners) from the moment it is written.
items.author: kshitijk4poor
items.summary: A bot-desktop fix makes lease acquisition stamp screen activity before writing the lease, so a human takeover counts as use of an idle screen. Previously a takeover landing on a long-idle screen during an idle check could cause the screen to be stopped under the human who just took it, with the lease handed back to the agent.
items.reasoning: Directly fixes a real user-facing race where a human taking over a desktop screen could have their session killed. Part of a large same-day cluster of desktop lease/idle fixes, signaling an active stabilization push.

items.title: Hermes Agent ElevenLabs: Make Sound Effects With the Official Plugin
items.content:
Hermes Agent ElevenLabs support just got a new trick: Nous Research released an official plugin called elevenlabs-sound-effects that lets Hermes turn a short text description into a real sound effect. You type “a heavy wooden door creaking open in a stone hall” and Hermes makes the audio file and sends it to you in chat. The plugin (v1.2.0) was added to the Hermes plugin catalog on 26 October 2026, and Nous announced it on X the next day as part of a growing set of “Game Dev Studio” tools for Hermes. Below I cover what it does, how to install it, every setting, what it costs to run, and how it fits next to the ElevenLabs voice you may already use in Hermes. I’ve also put one of my Hermes walkthrough videos below.

Key takeaways

One tool, elevenlabs_sound_effect: text in, sound file out (0.5 to 30 seconds, optional seamless loop).
Install with hermes plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects.
Uses the same ELEVENLABS_API_KEY as Hermes’ ElevenLabs voice.
Ships a sound-design skill, a free local ffmpeg script and a Desktop sound library.
Want this working in your business? Claim a free strategy session.






What the Hermes Agent ElevenLabs plugin does
The plugin connects Hermes to the ElevenLabs Sound Effects API. According to the catalog page, it adds exactly one tool to your agent: elevenlabs_sound_effect. You describe a sound in plain English and Hermes generates an audio file between 0.5 and 30 seconds long. It can also make the sound a seamless loop, which matters for things like background music, engine hums or rain.
Examples straight from the README:

“Glass shattering on a tile floor”
“A short retro coin pickup blip”
“90s hip-hop drum loop, 90 BPM, loopable”
“The sound of a heavy wooden door creaking open in a stone hall”

Hermes picks the details for each sound itself: the description (up to 450 characters — longer prompts are refused before anything is sent), the length, whether it loops, and a prompt_influence value from 0 to 1. A higher value follows your words more literally; a lower one gives more variety. You can also ask for a specific model on a single sound.
It’s an Official plugin, maintained by NousResearch, listed under Tools, and it needs Hermes 0.22.0 or newer. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, and its only Python dependency is httpx, which Hermes already ships.
How to install the ElevenLabs plugin in Hermes
Installing takes one command. Here are the steps, in order:

Make sure you’re on Hermes 0.22.0 or later (hermes update if you’re not sure).
Run hermes plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects. You can also install it straight from the hermes-official-plugins repo with hermes plugins install NousResearch/hermes-official-plugins#elevenlabs-sound-effects.
If ELEVENLABS_API_KEY isn’t set yet, the installer asks for it. You create a key in ElevenLabs under Profile → API keys.
The tool only shows up for the agent once the key is set.

Two details catch people out:

Plugins are per profile. If you run several Hermes profiles, install it on each one you want, for example hermes -p <profile> plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects.
Restricted keys need the right permission. If your ElevenLabs key is restricted, turn on the Sound Effects permission. It’s separate from the Text to Speech permission.

Prefer not to touch the terminal? Ask your agent: “Install the elevenlabs-sound-effects plugin on this profile and check the key works.”

Hermes ElevenLabs settings explained
In Hermes Desktop, open Capabilities → Plugins and click the gear icon on the plugin. Everywhere else, use hermes config set. These are the four settings the README lists:




Setting
Default
Options and notes




api_key
(unset)
Stored in .env as ELEVENLABS_API_KEY


sound_model
eleven_text_to_sound_v2
eleven_text_to_sound_v2 or eleven_text_to_sound_v3


output_format
mp3_44100_128
mp3_44100_128, mp3_44100_192, opus_48000_128, opus_48000_192, wav_44100, wav_48000


api_base_url
https://api.elevenlabs.io
Change only for an ElevenLabs data-residency endpoint, e.g. https://api.eu.residency.elevenlabs.io




For example, to switch to the v3 sound model:
hermes config set plugins.entries.elevenlabs-sound-effects.settings.sound_model eleven_text_to_sound_v3
And to get 48 kHz WAV files:
hermes config set plugins.entries.elevenlabs-sound-effects.settings.output_format wav_48000
Watch your ElevenLabs plan. The README notes that ElevenLabs documents 192 kbps MP3 for the Creator plan and above, and 44.1 kHz WAV for Pro and above. If your plan refuses a format, the tool simply reports ElevenLabs’ error back to you.
Where your sounds go and how they reach you
Every sound is saved under your Hermes home in cache/generated/audio/, with a file name built from the description, a timestamp and an ID, so nothing is ever overwritten. Each generation also adds one line to a sounds.jsonl log in the plugin’s own data folder: the prompt, length, model, format, file size and the credits ElevenLabs billed. That log stays on your machine.
Delivery depends on where you’re chatting:

Telegram, Discord, Slack and other messaging apps: the tool hands the agent a MEDIA: line, and the file arrives as an attachment.
MP3 (the default) plays inline on most chat apps. Ogg Opus and WAV can arrive as plain files — Telegram shows them that way.
Discord: Hermes releases after v0.22.5 send MP3 and WAV as normal attachments that play inline.
Terminal: you get the file path.
Hermes Desktop: you get a sound card (below).

So if you run Hermes on a VPS and talk to it on Telegram, you can ask for a sound from your phone and get it back in the same chat.
The sound-design skill and the free ffmpeg script
The plugin also bundles a skill called elevenlabs-sound-design. It teaches Hermes how to write good ElevenLabs prompts (based on ElevenLabs’ own prompting guide), make loops, choose a format for where the sound is going — a game engine, a video, an app interface or a chat — and build a sound pack.
Inside that skill is sfx_tool.py, a local post-processing script that uses ffmpeg. It can downmix to mono, trim silence, normalise loudness, add fades, check a loop seam for clicks, convert between OGG, WAV and MP3, and pack a named set into a folder with a manifest.json and a zip. It can also build a game “variation set” with matched loudness, such as three gravel footsteps.
The important part: this processing costs no ElevenLabs credits, because it runs on your own machine. You pay ElevenLabs once to generate a sound, then tidy it up for free. One example from the README:
python3 sfx_tool.py pack t1.wav t2.wav t3.wav --name "Footstep Gravel" --out-dir . --variations
You don’t need to run this yourself. Just ask Hermes: “Make three gravel footstep variations, mono, levelled, packed as OGG.”

Hermes Desktop: sound card and sound library
If you use Hermes Desktop, the plugin adds two things. The Desktop half is opt-in: open Capabilities → Plugins, switch to list view and turn on Desktop: ElevenLabs Sound Effects. Without it, Desktop still plays every sound in its built-in player.

Sound card: each sound shows in chat with a waveform, play/pause, a gapless loop toggle so you can hear the seam, download in each format, reveal in your file manager, and “Next” actions — 3 variations, shorter, longer, make it loop, or try the other model. Each Next row shows its cost, and nothing is billed until the agent actually runs the tool.
Sound library: press ⌘K and choose ElevenLabs: open sound library. You get every sound the active profile made, with its prompt and settings, a format filter and a prompt search. You can replay, download, reuse a prompt or jump back to the chat that made it.

The sound card needs a Hermes Desktop with tool-media renderers; the README says that arrives in the first release after v0.22.5. Older Desktops use the built-in player instead. Running Hermes on a remote machine? Install the plugin there and also into your Desktop via Capabilities → Plugins → Install from Git, with Desktop UI checked.
What it costs and what leaves your machine
Every call is a paid ElevenLabs generation on your own ElevenLabs account. The README reports what it was billed while testing: about 10 credits per second when a length is set, and a flat amount (about 50 credits) per generation when ElevenLabs picks the length. Loops can come back a little longer than requested, and the tool reports the real length next to the one you asked for. Check ElevenLabs’ own pricing for your plan.
Privacy is simple: only the sound description and its parameters are sent to ElevenLabs, with your API key. Nothing else from your conversation goes with it. Format conversions and the processing script run locally.
Who should use the Hermes ElevenLabs sound plugin
Nous framed this release as part of a “Game Dev Studio” suite, so game builders are the obvious fit. But it’s useful well beyond games:




You make…
Use it for




Games
Footsteps, pickups, UI blips, ambient loops and variation packs


Videos and Shorts
Whooshes, hits, transitions and background beds


Apps and websites
Short interface sounds in the right format


Podcasts and ads
Intros, stingers and scene sounds




If you already use Hermes for 3D work, it pairs naturally with the Meshy plugin I covered in Hermes Meshy: models from one plugin, sounds from the other, all from the same agent.
ElevenLabs sound effects vs ElevenLabs voice in Hermes
Hermes already supports ElevenLabs for text-to-speech — that’s the voice your agent speaks with. This plugin is different: it makes sound effects and music loops, not speech. The good news is they share the same key. If your ElevenLabs voice is already set up in Hermes, the installer finds ELEVENLABS_API_KEY and there’s nothing to enter.
For more on giving your agent a voice, read my guide to Hermes Apollo Voice.
My verdict on Hermes Agent ElevenLabs sound effects
This is a tidy, well-built plugin. One tool, clear settings, a skill that knows how to prompt, and a free local script for the fiddly editing work. The Desktop sound library is a nice touch for anyone making lots of sounds. Watch your credits, start with MP3, and if you build games, videos or apps, Hermes Agent ElevenLabs sound effects are worth installing today.
About Julian Goldie
I’m Julian Goldie — founder of Goldie Agency and the AI Profit Boardroom. I test new AI agents almost every day for 432K+ YouTube subscribers and run Hermes, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Claude and Codex side by side in my own Agent OS. Claim your free strategy session or join the AI Profit Boardroom.

FAQ: hermes agent elevenlabs
What is the Hermes Agent ElevenLabs plugin?
It’s the official elevenlabs-sound-effects plugin from Nous Research. It adds one tool, elevenlabs_sound_effect, that turns a text description into an audio file from 0.5 to 30 seconds, optionally as a seamless loop.
How do I install ElevenLabs sound effects in Hermes?
Run hermes plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects. The installer asks for your ElevenLabs API key if it isn’t set. Plugins are per profile, so use hermes -p <profile> plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects for other profiles.
Do I need a separate ElevenLabs key for sound effects?
No. It uses the same ELEVENLABS_API_KEY as Hermes’ ElevenLabs voice. If your key is restricted, enable the Sound Effects permission, which is separate from Text to Speech.
Does the Hermes ElevenLabs plugin cost money?
Each sound is a paid ElevenLabs generation billed to your ElevenLabs account. The bundled ffmpeg script and Desktop format conversions run locally and cost no credits.
Can Hermes send the sounds to Telegram or Discord?
Yes. The file is sent as an attachment on Telegram, Discord, Slack and other messaging platforms. MP3 plays inline on most chat apps; in Hermes Desktop it shows as a sound card.

And to get 48 kHz WAV files:

hermes config set plugins.entries.elevenlabs-sound-effects.settings.output_format wav_48000

Watch your ElevenLabs plan. The README notes that ElevenLabs documents 192 kbps MP3 for the Creator plan and above, and 44.1 kHz WAV for Pro and above. If your plan refuses a format, the tool simply reports ElevenLabs’ error back to you.

Where your sounds go and how they reach you

Every sound is saved under your Hermes home in cache/generated/audio/, with a file name built from the description, a timestamp and an ID, so nothing is ever overwritten. Each generation also adds one line to a sounds.jsonl log in the plugin’s own data folder: the prompt, length, model, format, file size and the credits ElevenLabs billed. That log stays on your machine.

Delivery depends on where you’re chatting:

Telegram, Discord, Slack and other messaging apps: the tool hands the agent a MEDIA: line, and the file arrives as an attachment.

MP3 (the default) plays inline on most chat apps. Ogg Opus and WAV can arrive as plain files — Telegram shows them that way.

Discord: Hermes releases after v0.22.5 send MP3 and WAV as normal attachments that play inline.

Terminal: you get the file path.

Hermes Desktop: you get a sound card (below).

So if you run Hermes on a VPS and talk to it on Telegram, you can ask for a sound from your phone and get it back in the same chat.

The sound-design skill and the free ffmpeg script

The plugin also bundles a skill called elevenlabs-sound-design. It teaches Hermes how to write good ElevenLabs prompts (based on ElevenLabs’ own prompting guide), make loops, choose a format for where the sound is going — a game engine, a video, an app interface or a chat — and build a sound pack.

Inside that skill is sfx_tool.py, a local post-processing script that uses ffmpeg. It can downmix to mono, trim silence, normalise loudness, add fades, check a loop seam for clicks, convert between OGG, WAV and MP3, and pack a named set into a folder with a manifest.json and a zip. It can also build a game “variation set” with matched loudness, such as three gravel footsteps.

The important part: this processing costs no ElevenLabs credits, because it runs on your own machine. You pay ElevenLabs once to generate a sound, then tidy it up for free. One example from the README:

python3 sfx_tool.py pack t1.wav t2.wav t3.wav --name "Footstep Gravel" --out-dir . --variations

You don’t need to run this yourself. Just ask Hermes: “Make three gravel footstep variations, mono, levelled, packed as OGG.”

Hermes Desktop: sound card and sound library

If you use Hermes Desktop, the plugin adds two things. The Desktop half is opt-in: open Capabilities → Plugins, switch to list view and turn on Desktop: ElevenLabs Sound Effects. Without it, Desktop still plays every sound in its built-in player.

Sound card: each sound shows in chat with a waveform, play/pause, a gapless loop toggle so you can hear the seam, download in each format, reveal in your file manager, and “Next” actions — 3 variations, shorter, longer, make it loop, or try the other model. Each Next row shows its cost, and nothing is billed until the agent actually runs the tool.

Sound library: press ⌘K and choose ElevenLabs: open sound library. You get every sound the active profile made, with its prompt and settings, a format filter and a prompt search. You can replay, download, reuse a prompt or jump back to the chat that made it.

The sound card needs a Hermes Desktop with tool-media renderers; the README says that arrives in the first release after v0.22.5. Older Desktops use the built-in player instead. Running Hermes on a remote machine? Install the plugin there and also into your Desktop via Capabilities → Plugins → Install from Git, with Desktop UI checked.

What it costs and what leaves your machine

Every call is a paid ElevenLabs generation on your own ElevenLabs account. The README reports what it was billed while testing: about 10 credits per second when a length is set, and a flat amount (about 50 credits) per generation when ElevenLabs picks the length. Loops can come back a little longer than requested, and the tool reports the real length next to the one you asked for. Check ElevenLabs’ own pricing for your plan.

Privacy is simple: only the sound description and its parameters are sent to ElevenLabs, with your API key. Nothing else from your conversation goes with it. Format conversions and the processing script run locally.

Who should use the Hermes ElevenLabs sound plugin

Nous framed this release as part of a “Game Dev Studio” suite, so game builders are the obvious fit. But it’s useful well beyond games:

You make…

Use it for

Games

Footsteps, pickups, UI blips, ambient loops and variation packs

Videos and Shorts

Whooshes, hits, transitions and background beds

Apps and websites

Short interface sounds in the right format

Podcasts and ads

Intros, stingers and scene sounds

If you already use Hermes for 3D work, it pairs naturally with the Meshy plugin I covered in Hermes Meshy: models from one plugin, sounds from the other, all from the same agent.

ElevenLabs sound effects vs ElevenLabs voice in Hermes

Hermes already supports ElevenLabs for text-to-speech — that’s the voice your agent speaks with. This plugin is different: it makes sound effects and music loops, not speech. The good news is they share the same key. If your ElevenLabs voice is already set up in Hermes, the installer finds ELEVENLABS_API_KEY and there’s nothing to enter.

For more on giving your agent a voice, read my guide to Hermes Apollo Voice.

My verdict on Hermes Agent ElevenLabs sound effects

This is a tidy, well-built plugin. One tool, clear settings, a skill that knows how to prompt, and a free local script for the fiddly editing work. The Desktop sound library is a nice touch for anyone making lots of sounds. Watch your credits, start with MP3, and if you build games, videos or apps, Hermes Agent ElevenLabs sound effects are worth installing today.

FAQ: hermes agent elevenlabs

What is the Hermes Agent ElevenLabs plugin?

It’s the official elevenlabs-sound-effects plugin from Nous Research. It adds one tool, elevenlabs_sound_effect, that turns a text description into an audio file from 0.5 to 30 seconds, optionally as a seamless loop.

How do I install ElevenLabs sound effects in Hermes?

Run hermes plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects. The installer asks for your ElevenLabs API key if it isn’t set. Plugins are per profile, so use hermes -p <profile> plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects for other profiles.

Do I need a separate ElevenLabs key for sound effects?

No. It uses the same ELEVENLABS_API_KEY as Hermes’ ElevenLabs voice. If your key is restricted, enable the Sound Effects permission, which is separate from Text to Speech.

Does the Hermes ElevenLabs plugin cost money?

Each sound is a paid ElevenLabs generation billed to your ElevenLabs account. The bundled ffmpeg script and Desktop format conversions run locally and cost no credits.

Can Hermes send the sounds to Telegram or Discord?

Yes. The file is sent as an attachment on Telegram, Discord, Slack and other messaging platforms. MP3 plays inline on most chat apps; in Hermes Desktop it shows as a sound card.

items.title: fix(bot-desktop): the idle stop of an abandoned human lease releases …
items.content:
fix(bot-desktop): the idle stop of an abandoned human lease releases that lease

Once a human lease lapses (four windows, ten minutes at least) the screen is stopped, but lease.json still
named the human, so computer_use and the browser refused with "a human has control" before anything
started the next screen: the docs' "the next use starts it again" did not hold. After that stop the
lease is released, but only the generation judged abandoned: lease.release() takes the epoch read before
the stop and does nothing if the lease changed since, so a takeover made while the screen was stopping
(another viewer, or the same viewer handing back and taking over again) is kept, and an abandoned lease
with no viewer id never turns into a bare release.
items.author: kshitijk4poor
items.summary: A bot-desktop fix ensures that when an idle stop closes a screen under an abandoned human lease, the lease itself is released so computer_use and the browser can start the next screen. The release is generation-guarded so a concurrent takeover made while the screen was stopping is preserved.
items.reasoning: Fixes a state bug where users got stuck with a human-has-control error after a screen stopped, but the scenario is an edge case following the new lease-lapse behavior. Part of the desktop idle cluster.

items.title: fix(bot-desktop): a killed sleep or check no longer ends the screen's…
items.content:
fix(bot-desktop): a killed sleep or check no longer ends the screen's self-stop

The watch loop inherited the launcher's set -e. A sleep killed from outside (a stray pkill, the OOM
killer) made wait fail and ended the loop silently, so that screen never stopped itself again. The
loop now runs with set +e: a killed sleep goes straight to the check, a failed check retries in 300 s.
A sleep that fails on its own (it cannot sleep at all) still ends the loop rather than spinning the check.
items.author: kshitijk4poor
items.summary: A bot-desktop fix removes inherited set -e from the screen watch loop so a killed sleep (for example from a stray pkill or the OOM killer) no longer silently ends the loop and disables self-stop. Failed checks now retry after 300 seconds while a sleep that cannot run still ends the loop.
items.reasoning: Prevents a silent, persistent failure mode where a screen would never stop itself again after an external kill signal. Reliability fix, though triggered only by uncommon events like OOM kills.
items.summary_html: A bot-desktop fix removes inherited set -e from the screen watch loop so a killed sleep (for example from a stray pkill or the OOM killer) no longer silently ends the loop and disables self-stop. items.title: fix(bot-desktop): a short idle window never times out a human between…
items.content:
fix(bot-desktop): a short idle window never times out a human between two viewer stamps

Review (Greptile P1): the human lease lapses after four idle windows, but an attached viewer stamps
activity at most once a minute (and the panel clock repaints once a minute), so stamps can be about
two minutes apart. With a short window (idle_stop_minutes: 0.1, four windows = 24 s) the idle stop
could close a screen a human was using between two stamps. The lapse is now four windows and never
less than 10 minutes (HUMAN_LEASE_ABANDONED_MIN_S). The default 30-minute window is unchanged (its
four windows are 2 h). Docs say so.

Test: with a 6 s window a human lease 150 s since the last stamp keeps the screen, and one past the
floor stops it; fails with the four-window lapse alone.
items.author: kshitijk4poor
items.summary: A bot-desktop fix guarantees the human lease lapse is at least 10 minutes (HUMAN_LEASE_ABANDONED_MIN_S) in addition to four idle windows, so very short idle windows can no longer time out an actively attached human between activity stamps. The default 30-minute window is unchanged.
items.reasoning: Prevents actively used sessions from being killed for anyone using aggressive idle_stop_minutes settings. User-facing fix flagged via review, but only affects non-default short-window configurations.

items.title: fix(bot-desktop): an infinite idle window is off and never fails start()
items.content:
fix(bot-desktop): an infinite idle window is off and never fails start()

idle_stop_minutes: .inf meant "never stop" before the self-stop. start() now computes the launcher's
first-check delay from the window, and next_check_in overflowed on an infinite one, so the screen
could not start. A non-finite or non-positive window now reads as off, like 0.
items.author: kshitijk4poor
items.summary: A bot-desktop fix makes a non-finite or non-positive idle_stop_minutes value behave as off (never stop), instead of overflowing next_check_in and preventing the screen from starting. The launcher's first-check delay is now computed from the configured window.
items.reasoning: Fixes a config corner case that could block screen startup for users setting an infinite idle window. Narrow but real, and it clarifies intended semantics for the idle window setting.
items.summary_html: A bot-desktop fix makes a non-finite or non-positive idle_stop_minutes value behave as off (never stop), instead of overflowing next_check_in and preventing the screen from starting. The launcher's first-check delay is now computed from the configured window.
